q: Which component does a PDA have that an NFA does not?
options: A stack alphabet Γ and an initial stack symbol Z₀
explain: A PDA is (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F). Γ and Z₀ describe the stack. NFAs already have final states and ε-moves.

q: The transition function of a PDA has the type…
options: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → finite subsets of Q × Γ*
explain: Each move depends on the state, the input symbol (or ε) and the top of the stack. It chooses a new state and a string to push in place of the top.

q: In the ID (q, w, γ) of a PDA, what are w and γ?
options: w is the unread input and γ is the stack contents, top first
w is the input already read and γ is the output
w is the stack and γ is the input
w is the next state and γ is the stack symbol
explain: An instantaneous description records the current state, what remains of the input, and the whole stack with its top on the left.

q: δ(q, a, X) contains (p, YX). What happens to the stack?
options: Y is pushed on top of X
X is popped and nothing is pushed
X is pushed on top of Y
explain: The top X is replaced by the string YX, whose leftmost symbol becomes the top. So Y now sits above X.

q: The PDA for aⁿbⁿ pushes A for each a, starting from stack Z₀. After reading aa, the stack (top first) is…
explain: (q₀, aabb, Z₀) ⊢ (q₀, abb, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₀, bb, AAZ₀). Each a adds one A on top.

q: Deterministic PDAs recognise exactly the same languages as nondeterministic PDAs.
explain: False. Unlike DFAs and NFAs, DPDAs are strictly weaker. For example, {wwᴿ} needs a guess about where the middle is.

q: Which language needs a PDA's nondeterminism (no DPDA accepts it)?
explain: With a centre marker c, the PDA knows when to switch from pushing to matching. Without one, it must guess where the middle is.

q: In the ID notation, what does (q, aw, Xβ) ⊢ (p, w, γβ) mean?
options: One move: read a, replace top X with γ, go to p
The PDA halts with an error
explain: ⊢ is a single move using (p, γ) ∈ δ(q, a, X). ⊢* would mean zero or more moves.

q: Why can a PDA recognise {aⁿbⁿ} when no DFA can?
options: Its stack acts as an unbounded counter
It can read the input backwards
It can write on its input
explain: Pushing one symbol per a and popping one per b compares the two counts, however large n is. A DFA only has finitely many states to count with.

q: The PDA for aⁿbⁿ reads aab. Where is it when the input runs out?
options: In q₁ with AZ₀ on the stack, so it rejects
In q₂ with Z₀, so it accepts
It is stuck before reading the b
explain: (q₀, aab, Z₀) ⊢ (q₀, ab, AZ₀) ⊢ (q₀, b, AAZ₀) ⊢ (q₁, ε, AZ₀). An A is still on top, so the ε-move on Z₀ to the final state cannot fire.
